extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially those crafting or revising first lines/paragraphs/pages/chapters)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for writing openings (first line, first paragraph, first page, chapter beginnings) that accurately promise and set reader expectations for the rest of a book or story. Emphasizes consistency, voice, revision, and appropriate signaling across media.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-line promise: prose quality and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The first line makes a promise about the prose quality and tone (e.g., if it promises beautiful and evocative prose, the rest of the book should deliver that level of writing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Name of the Wind's opening ('It was night again...a silence of three parts') promises 'beautiful and evocative prose.' If the middle of the book is suddenly dry or workmanlike, the opening's promise is broken. Use the first line intentionally to telegraph the book's voice and sustain that level throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openings should signal the book's range/genre expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening (first line/paragraph/page/prologue/pilot) should indicate what sort of experience the reader/viewer is signing up for — action, romance, contemplative prose, horror, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In television and some books, pilots/prologues often show characters at extremes (most violent or romantic) to demonstrate the show's or book's range (Lower Decks example). In books, packaging (cover, back blurb) also sets expectations, but the opening still needs to promise the right things that match genre and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise must match the book's actual tone and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't telegraph an experience in the opening that the body of the work does not deliver (e.g., an exciting opening for a contemplative novel will create a mismatch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your book is contemplative and quiet, the opening should be contemplative and quiet. Mismatches cause readers to put the book down. Ensure pacing and tonal promises made at the start reflect the book as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of voice across beginning and middle
rubrics_metrics.description: The voice established in the beginning should match the voice readers encounter in the middle of the book; voice is an amalgam of word choice, tone, and character voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find the book's voice and revise the beginning to ensure it matches. A useful check is flipping to the middle to sample the voice and then adjusting the opening so the promise is accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use revisions to create and maintain consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Revision is the primary tool for ensuring the opening's promise is one you can keep and that the book maintains consistent tone, pacing, and voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revising chapter openings and returning to early material after producing later material helps smooth changes in style or skill. Example: an author drew some later illustrations first and revisited earlier ones to ensure consistent style and stamina effects were smoothed out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat chapter beginnings as opportunities for mini-openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Each chapter beginning (page turn) is a chance to write a powerful first line that either reinforces the original promise or deliberately expands it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the chapter's first line hooks because it plants a hook, is pithy, or describes something in a new way. Use different strategies across chapter openings to maintain interest while staying consistent with the book's promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overwrought or 'purple' openings you can't sustain
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't make the beginning so ornate or elevated that you cannot maintain that tone or level of prose through the rest of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the opening is 'gorgeous and beautiful' but the rest is much weaker, the series/book can fall flat (example: author sold a three-book deal on first chapters that were later edited out, leaving a mismatch). Edit openings down or alter them to be representative of the full work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check mid-book samples to verify promises
rubrics_metrics.description: Sampling a middle page or chapter is an effective diagnostic to see whether the beginning's promise is fulfilled in the body of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Megan's friend habit: flip to the middle and read a page to judge the author's voice. If the middle is drastically different, revise the opening or the middle to create consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage tent-poles and connective material to avoid dips
rubrics_metrics.description: If a writer places tent-pole scenes (set pieces they love) and leaves dull connective material between them, readers will experience dips in engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either remove a weak tent-pole or enrich the connective canvas to keep readers engaged while connecting exciting scenes. Be conscious of which scenes you must keep and how to make transitions compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal future progression or arc appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Openings can legitimately show characters at extremes to promise future progression (e.g., a game opening showing full power that later represents an endpoint the player will work toward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an opening to promise an arc (e.g., a protagonist will grow from novice to master). Examples: video games and some novels open with high-action sequences to promise eventual power/skill development; Borderlands 2 mission text explicitly tells the player what will come later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be conscious and deliberate about the promises you make
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should intentionally craft the promises in their openings and regularly check whether they're keeping them as the work evolves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What is the promise of the premise? Are you still bringing the same level of fire and excitement to the remainder of your book as in the polished beginning? Homework suggestion: write six first lines that make promises you don't think you can keep, then analyze why and how to change them.
